title: Toldot: room at last (Genesis 26:18–22)
hook: wells named Quarrel and Enmity, then Rehoboth, broad places

segments.voice: Yesterday, two nations in one womb, the field and the tent. Your line was two in one womb. Did you name both sides of something? Day one hundred eighty-eight.

The parking spot. The armrest on the plane. The neighbor's hedge that's six inches over the line. Some fights are about real things. A lot of them are about who gets the space. Isaac, grown now, is living among the Philistines in a dry land, and in a dry land, water is everything. His father Abraham once dug wells there. Since then, they've been stopped up with earth. So Isaac starts digging. And every time he finds water, somebody shows up to claim it. Today: room at last.
screen: `WHO GETS THE SPACE?` → `WATER IN A DRY LAND.` → `ISAAC STARTS DIGGING.`

segments.voice: First, Isaac digs again the wells of his father, and here's a tender detail: he calls them by the same names his father had called them. Then his servants dig in the valley and find living water, a spring. The herdsmen of Gerar come and say: the water is ours. So Isaac names that well Esek, which means contention. Quarrel. And he moves on. They dig another well. Another fight. He names that one Sitnah, enmity. And he moves on again. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't fight for the first well, or the second. He gives each one an honest name, a record of what happened there, and he walks. Then they dig a third well, and this time, the text says, they didn't strive for it. He names it Rehoboth, from the Hebrew for broad, wide, open spaces. And he says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land." Room. That's the gift at the end of all that digging. The medieval commentator Ramban read the three wells as a picture of Jewish history, two that were fought over and a third, in the future, with room at last. Other readers keep it close to home. Some fights aren't worth winning. Moving on isn't the same as losing. And there's usually a Rehoboth somewhere, if you're willing to keep digging. The story ends with a surprise. The king of the Philistines comes to Isaac and asks for a treaty. The man who walked away twice ends up with peace.
screen: `HIS FATHER'S WELLS, HIS FATHER'S NAMES.` · `ESEK: QUARREL. SITNAH: ENMITY.` · `REHOBOTH: BROAD PLACES.` · `THE KING COMES ASKING FOR PEACE.` · then, large: `THE LORD HATH MADE ROOM FOR US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk away from one needless fight. Settle, and breathe. Think of one running quarrel in your life. A group chat argument. A turf war at work. A family thing about who's right. Ask yourself honestly: is this a well worth fighting for, or an Esek? If it's an Esek, picture yourself naming it, and walking on. Breathe into the open space on the other side. The bell holds the time.
Toldot. Generations: the portion where Isaac digs his father's wells, walks away from two fights, and finds Rehoboth, room at last.
Your line: there's room. Today, when you feel yourself gearing up for a small fight over space or credit, let it go, and look for the wider place. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching prizes pursuing peace and avoiding needless quarrels, machloket, and Rehovot, a city in Israel, takes its name from Isaac's well of broad places.

fork.setup: you've dug a well in a dry land and found water. the local herdsmen say it's theirs. you're Isaac. what do you do?
options: fight for it: you dug it.
name it quarrel, and dig somewhere else.
share it and hope for the best.
fork.reveal: Isaac named it Esek, quarrel, and moved on, twice, until he found Rehoboth, where nobody fought, and there was room.

original.note: Hebrew: broad places, wide spaces. the well where there was room at last.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dispute over water rights.
what it means: a man who names his quarrels honestly, walks away from them, and finds room.
what a scholar hears: Ramban reads the three wells as the Temples: two fought over and destroyed, the third still to come.
